newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed mostly lower as the market took a breather from recent gains. January lost $10 to close at $1,436 a tonne, while March lost $4 to close at $1,384 per tonne. Trade sources said the market looked friendly as long as January holds above the key support of $1,415. In New York coffee futures ended higher buoyed by commission house buying. December added 2.70 cents/lb to close at 122.25 cents/lb, while March closed 1.30 cents/lb higher at 113.95 cents/lb. The outer months added 1.00 to 1.20 cents/lb. The constant fall in consumer stocks continued to aid sentiment. There was also talk of Central Americans being able to sell coffee out through mid-1997 at a continued premium suggesting ongoing concerns about supply availability well into the season. Another encouraging factor was a report that Brazilian production is likely to fall in 1997/98. However, it may be a little bit premature to give any firm estimate. Many traders believe that the market will maintain its uptrend through the end of December, but thereafter the outlook is more uncertain.

UGANDA - According to official sources coffee production in 1996/97 (October/September) is likely to reach 3.750 million 60-kg bags up from 3.650 million bags the previous year. The Uganda Coffee Development Authority (UCDA) said that exports in 1996/97 are likely to fall to 3.6 million bags down from a record 4.15 million bags exported in 1995/96. Originally exports were expected to be higher but damage caused by hail in some growing districts as well as the coffee wilt disease forced UCDA to lower the export forecast. UCDA said export earnings in 1995/96 fell in real terms by 10.1 per cent to $388.9 million from $432.0 million in 1994/95 when exports were at 2.793 million bags. UCDA blamed the decline in export revenue to lower world market prices. Another factor, according to UCDA, was the adoption of the just-in-time buying strategy by roasters in 1994 after the frost in Brazil. It said the strategy was given further support by improved transportation systems in producing countries.

ETHIOPIA - Trade and Industry Minister Kasahun Ayele told Reuters television that low coffee prices have caused Ethiopia's export earnings to fall by more than 7 per cent to $440.4 million in 1995/96 (July/June). Ethiopia earned $279.5 million from exporting a record 1.700 million bags of coffee in 1995/96 compared to $330.9 million from 1.307 million bags in 1994/95, Kasahun said. Coffee accounted for more than 60 percent of foreign exchange earnings in 1995/96. Kasahun added that despite the setback from lower coffee prices, Ethiopia's total export drive had shown fast growth since the government of Prime Minister Meles Zenawi launched an economic liberalization programme in 1992.

GERMANY - Germany imported 1.159 million bags of coffee in July 1996 nearly 19 percent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 7.563 million bags, 4 percent more than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 5.7 percent to 12.9 million bags. Major suppliers of green coffee in January/July 1996 were El Salvador (706,700 vs 636,800 bags), Honduras (445,600 vs 371,700 bags), and Vietnam (424,500 vs 455,400 bags). The country exported 1.987 million bags of coffee in January/July 1996, 17 percent more than was exported the same period in 1995. Total exports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 7.9 percent to 3.238 million bags.
